strengths: Extensive real-world validation: over 2,000 robot rollouts across four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, with per-object and per-stage breakdowns (Tables 11-14) that give a fine-grained picture of where tactile sensing helps.

The plugin tactile adapter is well-motivated and empirically supported: the ablation (Table 5) cleanly separates coupled injection (DECO.cs), decoupled-from-scratch (DECO.ds), and the parameter-efficient plugin (DECO.p), showing that naive concatenation-style fusion fails while decoupled cross-attention injection succeeds, and that the adapter matches from-scratch performance with only 7.97M trainable parameters.
The analysis distinguishing weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant tasks (pick-and-place/sorting vs. waste disposal/assembly) is a useful and honest finding with practical value for the community.

Release of DECO-50 (50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K trajectories of bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile and active vision) addresses a genuine gap, as no existing dataset combines bimanual + dexterous hands + tactile sensing at scale (Table 9); data collection setup and object reproducibility details are provided.
Training details, hyperparameters, baseline re-implementation choices (LeRobot, capacity-matched DP), and deployment conditions are documented in sufficient detail to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the components (DiT blocks with AdaLN conditioning, cross-attention injection, LoRA adaptation, flow matching) are all well-established; the contribution is their combination and engineering rather than a new mechanism, and the central 'decoupled conditioning' hypothesis is asserted more than theoretically grounded.

No statistical rigor on the real-world evaluations: with 10-20 trials per cell, differences of a few successes (e.g., DECO 103/120 vs. ACT 101/120 on Task 1) are within plausible noise, yet aggregate improvement claims (21% over baseline) are stated without confidence intervals or significance tests.

Baselines are weak and limited to ACT and DP; no comparison against existing tactile-aware policies (e.g., Reactive Diffusion Policy, ViTacFormer, VT-Refine) that are cited as closely related, so the claim that decoupled fusion is the right approach for tactile is not tested against the strongest alternatives.
The claim that the tactile adapter 'can be incorporated into any pretrained vision-based policy' (Conclusion) is untested — it is only applied to DECO itself, not to ACT, DP, or any other backbone.

Models are trained independently per task with a one-hot task/object condition, which undercuts framing as a general policy and leaves long-horizon and cross-task generalization unexplored (acknowledged as future work, but the OOD object results in Table 12 are only reported for material sorting and are partially omitted for baselines).

Minor presentation issues reduce trust: Table 4 reports a total of '55/100' although the maximum should be 80; some delta computations in Table 1 are inconsistent in what baseline they compare against; Eq. 4's gating mechanism is described in text but the equation does not reflect the stated concatenation/gating structure.

Significance is somewhat specialized: the dataset is collected on a specific embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands) and the evaluation is confined to that platform, limiting immediate broader impact compared to cross-embodiment resources.

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation: the paper reports results across four tasks with a large number of rollouts (120 trials per method on Tasks 1-2, 80 on Tasks 3-4), plus out-of-distribution object evaluations in the appendix, which is more thorough than many manipulation papers.

The paper clearly distinguishes weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant tasks and shows when tactile data does and does not help, which is an honest and useful empirical finding for practitioners deciding whether tactile collection is justified.

The ablation design is meaningful: comparing coupled tactile injection (DECO.cs), decoupled injection trained from scratch (DECO.ds), and the plugin adapter (DECO.p) directly tests the central design claim about injection mechanism rather than just modality presence.

The two-stage adapter result (7.97M trainable parameters, comparable performance to training from scratch on the ablation pairs) is a practically relevant demonstration of parameter-efficient modality addition.

The DECO-50 dataset (real bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing and active vision) addresses a genuine gap, and the dataset comparison table and collection details are reasonably documented.
weaknesses: Limited and outdated baselines: the only comparisons are ACT and DP, both from 2023, re-implemented with modified architectures. There are no comparisons against modern visuo-tactile policies (e.g., Reactive Diffusion Policy, ViTacFormer, TouchVLA, VT-Refine) or even RDT-1B, despite the related-work section discussing them. The claim of 'best performance' is therefore weakly supported against the current state of the art.

No statistical rigor: results are single-seed point estimates with 10-20 trials per condition and no error bars, seeds, or significance analysis. Several key conclusions rest on differences of a few trials (e.g., DECO 103/120 vs. ACT 101/120 on Task 1; DECO.ds 17/20 vs. DECO.p 17/20 vs. 18/20 on individual ablation stages), which may easily be within run-to-run variance.

Inconsistencies across tables undermine trust in the results: the main-text Table 3 reports DP.t Stage 2 at 65/80 while the appendix Table 13 reports 43/80 for the same condition; Table 4's total reads 55/100 where all entries are out of 80; the Table 12 OOD total row is mangled and inconsistent with the appendix decomposition.

The core method is an assembly of known components (DiT with AdaLN conditioning from Peebles & Xie, joint self-attention à la MMDiT/SD3, cross-attention for an extra modality, LoRA adapters), and the novelty of 'decoupled conditioning' is conceptual rather than technical; the decoupling claim is validated only on two assembly object pairs with small sample sizes.

Generalization claims exceed evidence: the paper states the tactile adapter 'can be incorporated into any pretrained vision-based policy' and 'larger-scale visual-language-action models,' but it is only demonstrated on the authors' own DECO backbone; a cross-architecture experiment is needed to support this claim.

The dataset contribution is smaller than the framing suggests: 50 hours / 8K episodes is modest relative to the datasets the paper positions itself against (RoboMIND 2.0, RoboCOIN, RH20T), and models are trained per-task rather than on the full corpus, which weakens the utility of the release as a general resource.

Presentation quality issues: several typos ('Traning Epochs', 'The only differences is'), a gate formulation in Eq. 4 whose description in text does not clearly match the equation (the gating mechanism controlling the two tactile feature branches is not visible in the formula), and occasional vague claims without quantitative support.

Reproducibility is partial: training hyperparameters are given, but there is no code release statement, no demonstration of inference-time sensitivity (e.g., number of flow-matching steps), and checkpoint selection via validation performance is not described in terms of how the validation set is constructed for single-task training regimes.

strengths: Substantial empirical effort: over 2,000 real-robot rollouts across four tasks with per-object, per-stage breakdowns and OOD generalization tests, which is rare and valuable for contact-rich bimanual manipulation.

DECO-50 is a genuinely useful resource: bimanual dexterous manipulation with dense tactile sensing (1,062 contact points), active binocular vision, and teleoperation at 30 Hz; the dataset comparison table (Table 9) clearly positions it against prior benchmarks.

The ablation design is well-conceived: DECO.cs (coupled fusion) vs. DECO.ds (decoupled, from scratch) vs. DECO.p (plugin adapter) directly tests the central claim that how tactile is injected matters, and the results (Table 5) support that coupled conditioning behaves like no tactile at all.

The plugin tactile adapter is practically compelling: 7.97M trainable parameters (~9% of the model) achieving performance comparable to training from scratch with tactile, demonstrated on a frozen pretrained policy.
Honest scoping of where tactile helps: the paper distinguishes weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant tasks rather than overclaiming universal benefit, and includes an appropriate Impact Statement.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the architecture combines well-known components (DiT/MMDiT-style blocks, AdaLN conditioning from Peebles & Xie, cross-attention, LoRA, flow matching). The 'decoupled conditioning' principle is a sensible design choice but is presented with more novelty than it warrants; no new theoretical insight or mechanism is introduced.

Baseline coverage is weak for the central claims. Only re-implemented ACT and DP are compared, while recent visuo-tactile policies and stronger diffusion policies (RDT-1B, pi0, ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy) are cited but not evaluated. The claim that DECO 'achieves the best performance across all tasks' is only established against two older baselines.

Attribution of gains is confounded: DECO differs from DP not only in 'decoupled' conditioning but also in backbone (ResNet-34 vs ResNet-18), sampler (flow matching vs DDIM), and inference steps (5 vs 10), while the paper attributes the improvement to the joint self-attention architecture. No ablation isolates these factors.

Table inconsistencies undermine confidence: Table 4's DECO.p total is given as 55/100 while all other cells and the appendix (Table 14) use /80; Table 3's 'Results' row simply repeats Stage 3 without explanation; Table 12 mixes evaluated and '–/20' OOD entries within one total row.
No statistical treatment: success rates are reported as single-run counts without confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates, which matters given margins of a few trials on 20-trial cells.

Methodological under-specification: Eq. 4 uses an undefined 'Sinusoid' function and the gating mechanism controlling the two tactile feature branches is described only vaguely, hurting reproducibility of the tactile encoder; code release is not explicitly promised.

Writing quality issues ('The only differences is', 'Traning Epochs', 'none which we feel') and some verbose/duplicated text in the ablation discussion suggest the paper needed another careful editing pass.

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 robot rollouts across four bimanual dexterous tasks, including per-object/stage breakdowns with Wilson 95% confidence intervals, which is unusually thorough for robot-learning papers

Well-designed ablations that directly test the central claims: coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds, Table 5), modality-to-pathway permutation showing dramatic degradation when assignments are swapped (Table 7, 0/40 vs. 29/40 on Stage 3), and a ResNet-18 vs. ResNet-34 control that reasonably rules out encoder capacity as the driver of gains

The plugin tactile adapter result (7.97M trainable parameters, comparable performance to training from scratch with tactile) is a practically useful contribution, and the two-stage paradigm cleanly separates vision-action pretraining from tactile adaptation

Release of DECO-50, a large bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing (50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K trajectories), filling a documented gap (Table 11 comparison); the appendix provides detailed sensor layouts, teleoperation setup, and reproducible 3D-printed objects
Honest limitations section identifying the single-hardware/single-sensor restriction and plans for validation on pretrained VLAs
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate: DECO assembles existing components (DiT, AdaLN conditioning from DiT, cross-attention, LoRA, flow matching) into a sensible configuration; the 'decoupled conditioning' hypothesis is supported empirically but the paper offers little mechanistic analysis of why the assignment works, beyond qualitative jitter observations

Baseline coverage is thin relative to the claims: comparisons are limited to ACT, DP, and DP.t (tactile concatenation), with no comparison to recent visuo-tactile policies cited in the related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion, VT-Refine, Higuera et al.'s adapter), so 'best performance across all tasks' is established only within a narrow set of baselines and only on the authors' own dataset

Evaluation protocol details raise potential bias concerns: models are selected as the 'best-performing checkpoint based on validation performance' without specifying how validation is measured (real rollouts vs. held-out loss), and training epochs differ substantially across methods (ACT 30 vs. DP 200 vs. DECO 150) without a discussion of baseline tuning fairness; per-object results also show high variance (e.g., DECO.p worse than DECO on several Task 1 objects)

All results are confined to the authors' own dataset and single hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands and normal-force-only piezoresistive sensors); no simulation or cross-embodiment experiments, and the tactile findings may be specific to this normal-force sensor modality

The dataset, while valuable, is modest relative to name ('DECO-50' = 50 hours) and is task-specific to four scenarios, limiting its use for generalist or cross-embodiment claims that the related-work positioning invokes

Minor presentation issues: typos ('The only differences is'), Eq. 4's sinusoid/gating formulation is under-explained (the text description and equation do not obviously match), and some tables lack explicit training-seed or trial-randomization details

strengths: Substantial empirical effort: over 2,000 real-robot rollouts across 4 bimanual dexterous tasks (28 sub-tasks), with per-object, per-stage success counts and Wilson 95% confidence intervals in the appendix, which exceeds the evaluation rigor of many robot-learning papers.

The DECO-50 dataset release (50 hours, ~5M frames, bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing and active vision) is a genuinely useful community resource, and Table 11 positions it well against prior datasets (DROID, RoboMIND, RoboCOIN, VTDexManip, etc.).

The ablations are targeted and informative: coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds, Table 5), the plugin adapter vs. training from scratch (Table 5/6), and the modality-to-pathway swap experiment (Table 7, 0/40 vs. 29/40 on Stage 3) provide evidence that the specific conditioning assignment matters.

The supplemental ResNet-18 experiments (Tables 17-20) address the obvious confound that DECO simply has a larger vision encoder than ACT/DP, and honest discussion of when tactile is not helpful (weakly tactile-relevant tasks).
Limitations are candidly discussed (single hardware platform, one hand/tactile sensor type, no temporal modeling), which is appropriate.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is an assembly of well-known components: DiT (Peebles & Xie 2023), AdaLN, joint self-attention between image and action tokens, cross-attention for auxiliary conditioning, and LoRA adaptation. The 'MMDiT' block closely mirrors Stable Diffusion 3's MMDiT, and no new training objective, algorithm, or theoretical insight is introduced; the contribution is a configuration choice plus a dataset.

The central 'decoupled conditioning' hypothesis is under-justified analytically. The claimed reasons (vision dominance, tactile sparsity, proprioception granularity) are plausible but asserted post hoc; the pathway-swap ablation (Table 7) is only run on two object pairs of one task, and the mechanistic explanation ('cross-attention treats each joint as a sequence element... causes jitter') is speculative and not analyzed (e.g., no attention maps, ablations over number of blocks receiving tactile input, or rank sensitivity for LoRA).

Baselines are weak and comparisons with the most relevant prior visuo-tactile policies are missing. ACT and DP are 2023-era methods; recent touch-integrated policies cited in Related Work (ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, Higuera et al. 2025, VT-Refine) are discussed but never compared against, even on the contact-rich tasks where tactile matters. The only tactile baseline, DP.t, is a strawman-style 'concatenate and retrain' variant.

Several headline claims are overstated or fragile. The '21% improvement' and '10.25% average success gain' are relative improvements computed on a single-task-per-object basis; many per-object differences lie inside overlapping Wilson intervals, and there is no statistical significance testing between DECO and DECO.p (e.g., 82.50% vs. 72.25%). The abstract's claim that the adapter brings gains 'while tuning less than 10% of the parameters' is fine, but the claim that DECO.p matches DECO.ds is contradicted in places by Table 5 (DECO.ds wins 37/40 vs. 36/40, 34/40 vs. 33/40).

Technical presentation issues undermine confidence: Eq. 4 for the tactile encoder is confusing and inconsistent with the surrounding text (the gating mechanism described verbally does not appear in the equation; the Sinusoid(sigma(W·T)·T) composition is unmotivated and looks like it may be mis-typed); Code/Project Page/Dataset links in the manuscript are empty, so reproducibility currently rests on promised release; typos ('Traning' in Table 12, 'Success Rate 13/24' footnotes) and inconsistent figures (Fig. 3 vs. Fig. 4 descriptions of adapter placement) suggest the paper was not carefully polished.
The OOD evaluation (Table 14) is conducted only for DECO variants; ACT/DP/DP.t are marked '–/20' with no explanation, making the generalization analysis asymmetric and hard to interpret.

No language conditioning and no comparison with any VLA-style model despite framing the problem in the VLA context; the choice of ResNet-34/512-dim/6-block backbone is not ablated beyond the ResNet-18 experiment, so the reported gains could partly reflect other unspecified architectural advantages over DP's FiLM conditioning.

Ethics/reproducibility materials are thin: the Impact Statement is boilerplate, the reproducibility checklist content (seeds, number of training reruns) is absent, and given that all results come from single training runs of real-robot policies, run-to-run variance is unquantified.

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation: over 2,000 rollouts across 4 scenarios and 28 sub-tasks, with per-object and per-stage breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals in the appendix, which is unusually thorough for a robot learning paper and supports the quantitative claims.

The ablation design is thoughtful and addresses the most obvious confounds: (i) DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds isolates coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection under identical preprocessing and training from scratch; (ii) the pathway-permutation experiment (Table 7) directly tests the central 'modality-specific injection matters' hypothesis and yields a dramatic, interpretable result (0/40 vs. 29/40 on Stage 3); (iii) the ResNet-18 vs. ResNet-34 study (Tables 17-20) rules out vision encoder capacity as the driver of DECO's advantage over DP.

The plugin tactile adapter result is practically significant: updating only 7.97M parameters (Table 6) while achieving performance comparable to DECO.ds trained from scratch is a useful, transferable finding for adding tactile sensing to pretrained visuomotor policies.

The DECO-50 dataset (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K trajectories, bimanual dexterous hands with tactile sensing and active vision) fills a genuine gap, as documented by the comparison table (Table 11), and the hardware/sensor details (Table 10, Appendix A.3) are described in reproducible detail.

The analysis distinguishes weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant tasks, which is honest and more informative than claiming tactile universally helps; the limitations section is candid about single-platform, single-sensor scope.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is narrow: the only external methods are ACT and DP (both without tactile by default), plus DP.t as a tactile baseline. None of the recent visuo-tactile policies the paper itself cites (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, Tactile-VLA, VT-Refine) are compared against, so the claim that DECO's decoupled fusion is superior to existing fusion approaches is never tested against an external implementation of those approaches.

All evaluation is on the authors' own tasks, hardware, and dataset. The generality of the decoupled-conditioning principle is only validated in one architecture, one embodiment, and one sensor type; there is no cross-dataset or cross-platform evidence, which limits how far others can build on the specific pathway-assignment conclusion (the limitations section acknowledges this).

In Table 5, DECO.ds (from scratch) slightly outperforms the plugin adapter DECO.p on some cells (e.g., 14/20 vs. 13/20 on 00296-2x Stage 3; 37/40 vs. 36/40), and on Stage 1 the tactile-free DECO actually beats all tactile variants (20/20 vs. 17-19/20). The paper treats DECO.p as 'comparable' but the margins are within noise and no statistical test is reported for these ablation comparisons; the number of training runs/seeds is not specified.

Reproducibility is asserted but not yet verifiable: the Code / Project Page / Dataset links on page 1 are empty placeholders in the manuscript, and the hyperparameter section points to 'the open-sourced code at .' As submitted, a reader cannot access code, weights, or data.

The mechanistic justification for the specific pathway assignment (vision via self-attention, proprioception via AdaLN, tactile via cross-attention) is somewhat post-hoc: the motivation is a hypothesis about modality roles, and the supporting permutation ablation covers only two object pairs of one task. The explanation for the permuted-model jitter (overemphasizing proprioception via cross-attention) is plausible but not directly measured.

Minor presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('The only differences is', 'Traning Epochs' in Table 12), some ablation cells mix bold/normal formatting inconsistently, and the DECO-50 naming (50 hours) is not explained; the claim of '21% improvement over the baseline' mixes percentage-point and relative formulations that should be stated consistently.

strengths: Substantial and well-executed real-world evaluation: over 2,000 rollouts across four bimanual dexterous tasks with per-object success counts, stage-wise breakdowns, and Wilson 95% confidence intervals in the appendix, which is unusually rigorous for real-robot policy evaluation.

The DECO-50 dataset (50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K successful trajectories of bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing and active vision) fills a genuine gap; the dataset comparison table (Table 11) honestly situates it against existing resources, most of which lack the combination of bimanual + dexterous + tactile + real data.

Well-designed ablations that actually test the paper's central claims: coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds), a pathway-swap experiment (Table 7) showing modality-to-pathway assignment matters dramatically (0/40 vs. 29/40 on Stage 3), and a ResNet-18 vs. ResNet-34 capacity control that rules out encoder capacity as the source of gains.

The plugin tactile adapter demonstrates a practically valuable result: tactile data can be added to a frozen pretrained visuomotor policy by tuning only 7.97M parameters while matching DECO.ds trained from scratch (e.g., 82.50% vs. 82.50% average, Table 1).

Broad additional simulation validation on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, and DexJoCo, with honest disclosure of confounds (e.g., UniVTAC baselines use large-scale pretraining, action-stride workaround for put_bottle_in_shelf) and a failure-mode analysis (timeout vs. slip).
Honest limitations section (single hardware platform, one sensor type, no multi-directional tactile evaluation).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: MMDiT is essentially a DiT combining known components (joint self-attention, AdaLN conditioning from DiT/Peebles & Xie, cross-attention for auxiliary modality, LoRA adaptation); the contribution is a well-engineered configuration rather than a new technique, and the 'decoupling hypothesis' is motivated by intuition more than analysis.

Baseline coverage on the real robot is narrow: only ACT and DP (plus DPt concatenation). No comparison to recent visuotactile policies (e.g., VT-Refine, MimicTouch, iFT, OmniVTLA, Touch-VLA) that the related-work section itself cites, so the claim of 'best performance across all tasks' is only established against older baselines.

The pathway-swap ablation (Table 7), which is the key evidence for the decoupling principle, is run on only one task (assembly, two object pairs); the generality of the modality-to-pathway claim would benefit from replication on the waste-disposal task and, ideally, in simulation where more trials are cheap.

Gains on weakly-tactile tasks are small and within confidence intervals (e.g., DECO 103/120 vs. ACT 101/120 on pick-and-place), so the headline '72.25% (+21%)' is driven almost entirely by contact-rich tasks; the paper is reasonably clear about this, but the abstract-level framing could overstate the general improvement.

Real-world data collection success rates in Table 8 are very high (often ~100%), suggesting fairly teleoperator-favorable, scripted data; the implications for policy robustness to more diverse or noisy demonstrations are not discussed.

Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated: code/dataset links are blank in the manuscript; hyperparameters and hardware details are otherwise thorough, and simulation code/weights are promised, but nothing is verifiable at review time.

The tactile sensing is normal-force-only piezoresistive; claims about detecting 'force-related signals' and fine-grained contact states are restricted to this sensing modality, and the paper does not test shear or tactile arrays with higher fidelity where decoupling might behave differently.

strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive systems contribution: a new architecture (DECO), a parameter-efficient tactile adapter, and a new real-world dataset (DECO-50) for bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing, a combination that is genuinely scarce in the literature (as their own Table 11 dataset comparison shows).

The real-world evaluation is unusually extensive: over 2,000 rollouts across 4 scenarios and 28 sub-tasks, with per-object breakdowns, Wilson 95% confidence intervals, and OOD object tests, which is above the evidential standard of most robot learning papers.

The ablations are well-targeted: comparing coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection (Table 5), swapping modality-to-pathway assignments (Table 7), and LoRA fine-tuning vs. training from scratch (Table 6) directly test the paper's central design claims rather than only headline numbers.

A supplementary experiment with a ResNet-18 encoder (Appendix B.3) controls for encoder capacity against the baselines, addressing the obvious confound that DECO outperforms baselines simply due to model size.

Evaluation extends beyond the authors' own dataset to four simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo), where DECO is competitive with much larger pretrained models despite having ~80M parameters, and the authors carefully flag where comparisons are not protocol-matched.

Limitations are honestly discussed (single hardware platform, one hand type and sensor, no cross-embodiment validation), and the paper distinguishes tasks that benefit from tactile vs. those that do not rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is modest. The 'decoupled' conditioning is essentially a recombination of established components: joint self-attention for vision/action tokens, AdaLN conditioning (Peebles & Xie, 2023), cross-attention for auxiliary modality, and LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). The conceptual claim that modalities 'contribute unequally and should influence the policy through distinct mechanisms' is plausible but supported only empirically, with limited analysis of why each pathway assignment works.

The key comparison conflating architecture and conditioning is incomplete. DP.t is the only tactile baseline, and it is a U-Net policy with naive concatenation trained from scratch. There is no experiment isolating the decoupled injection scheme within the DP architecture, so the claim that the decoupled paradigm (rather than the MMDiT backbone, flow matching, longer training, etc.) drives the improvements is not fully disentangled.

The DP baseline appears weakened: the authors deliberately reduced DP's U-Net channels from [512,1024,2048] to [256,512,1024] 'to ensure comparable model capacity.' DP's poor performance (51.25% overall) may partly reflect this modification, and the near-200-epoch training regime favors models tuned on the authors' own setup.

The tactile adapter's generality is undercut by its own simulation results: on UniVTAC, DECO and DECO.p are identical at 82.1% average (Table 23), with the adapter slightly degrading some tasks (e.g., insert hole 63.0->59.0), so the headline 10.25% adapter gain rests on a single platform and sensor.

Checkpoint selection is 'best-performing checkpoint based on validation performance' (Appendix B.1). If validation conditions mirror deployment, this is defensible, but the procedure is not described precisely enough to rule out optimistic selection, and per-object results (e.g., DECO.p losing to DECO on several Task 1 objects) suggest high variance not fully captured by the analysis.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the Code/Project Page/Dataset links in the title block and Appendix B.1 are empty placeholders, so reproducibility currently depends entirely on promised releases; there are minor inconsistencies (e.g., DECO with ResNet-18 outperforming ResNet-34 on several tasks is described as 'marginal' but not explained; Table 15's Paper Ball Stage 2/3 for DP.t is internally inconsistent with Table 3).

The paper claims the dataset 'will serve as a valuable resource,' but at 50 hours / 8K trajectories it is small relative to the cited scale benchmarks (RoboMIND 2.0 at 1000+ hours, 310K episodes), so its impact depends on the actual release of data and code.

strengths: Extensive and credible real-world evaluation: over 2,000 robot rollouts across four bimanual dexterous tasks with per-object/per-stage breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, which is substantially more thorough than typical policy papers.

Thoughtful ablation design: the coupled-vs-decoupled tactile injection comparison (DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p in Table 5), the modality-to-pathway permutation ablation (Table 7, dramatic 0/40 vs 29/40 drop on Stage 3), and the ResNet-18 vs ResNet-34 control (Appendix B.3) collectively support the central claim that *how* a modality is injected matters, beyond generic model capacity.

The parameter-efficiency result is convincing: DECO.p achieves performance comparable to training from scratch (DECO.ds) while updating only 7.97M parameters (<10% of the model), a practically useful finding for adding tactile sensing to pretrained visuomotor policies.

Release of DECO-50, a bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K trajectories), addresses a genuine gap identified in the related-work survey (Table 11 comparison is informative).

Additional evaluation on four simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) shows competitive performance against much larger VLA baselines, going beyond a single self-collected testbed.

Honest limitations section: the authors explicitly acknowledge single-hardware-platform restriction, one hand/sensor type, and the need to validate the adapter on larger VLAs, and they honestly report tasks where tactile provides no benefit (Pick and Place, most of Material Sorting).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core architecture is a fairly direct assembly of established components (DiT-style AdaLN conditioning from Peebles & Xie, joint self-attention, cross-attention for auxiliary modality, LoRA adapters, flow matching). The 'decoupled' design principle is intuitive rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and its superiority rests mainly on the paper's own ablations.

Baselines are relatively weak and dated: real-world comparisons are limited to ACT and DP (plus a naive DP.t concatenation variant). No comparison against existing visuo-tactile policies the paper itself cites (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, Tactile-VLA-style approaches) on the real robot, so the claim that DECO's decoupling beats alternative fusion schemes is only tested against the authors' own DECO.cs variant.

Some experimental asymmetries raise questions: DP's U-Net channels were reduced from the default to 'a similar parameter scale,' and DP uses DDIM with 10 steps while DECO uses flow matching with 5 steps; the stated rationale (inference speed) is plausible but these tuning choices could advantage DECO.

Generalization evidence is thin relative to the framing: evaluation is confined to one robot (Unitree H1-2), one hand (Inspire RH56DFTP), one tactile sensor type, and fixed scene setups; the OOD object tests in Table 14 are a positive step but limited in scope.

Writing/reproducibility gaps: the tactile encoder equation (Eq. 4) is described with a 'gating mechanism' whose relationship to the Figure 4 diagram is unclear; placeholder fields for Code/Project Page/Dataset links are blank in the manuscript, and several cited works are preprints, limiting verifiability of claims at review time.

Claim calibration: headline numbers ('21% improvement over the baseline', '10.25% additional average success rate') aggregate over tasks where tactile demonstrably does not help, so the per-task story is more nuanced than the abstract implies, though the body text is appropriately transparent about this.
